terms.means: Cut into small cubes about the size of a pea. Try to make them all close to the same size so they cook evenly.
Chop into tiny bits, smaller than a grain of rice. Keep rocking the knife back and forth over the pile until nothing big is left.
Cut into rough, bite-size pieces. They don't have to match.
Cut into flat pieces, like slices of bread.
Cut into thin sticks, about the size of a matchstick.
Rub food down a grater so it falls off in shreds. The big holes make shreds. The small holes make a paste.
Grate just the colored outside of a lemon or orange peel. Stop when you see white; the white part tastes bitter.
Cook a liquid with small, lazy bubbles that pop now and then. If big bubbles roll all over, turn the heat down.
Big bubbles rolling all over the pot, even while you stir.
Cook gently in liquid that's barely bubbling.
Cook in a little hot oil or butter, stirring often.
Cook in a very hot pan without moving the food, so the outside turns deep brown.
Brown the food first, then cook it slowly with a little liquid and the lid on until it's very tender.
Soak food in a flavorful liquid, called a marinade, before you cook it.
Stir fast in little circles with a whisk or a fork, to mix things together and add air.
Beat soft butter and sugar together hard until the mixture is fluffy and a little paler.
Lay the dough over itself in layers, like folding a letter to fit in an envelope.
Push the dough away with the heel of your hand, fold it back, turn it, and repeat until it's smooth and stretchy.
Sprinkle a thin, light layer, like flour on the counter so dough doesn't stick.
Gently lift and turn the food so every piece gets coated, like tossing a salad.
Hot oil looks wavy and rippled on top. That means it's hot enough for the food.
Meat has thin lines running through it, like the lines in wood. Cut across those lines, not along them, so each bite is tender.
Butter and flour cooked together, stirring, for a few minutes. It thickens milk or broth into a smooth sauce. Say it "roo."
